**Y components (which bit each one reads).** In each known task, one bit splits the two buttons cleanly:
- In X3-Y1-Z2, every input that gets button 3 has bit 2 equal to (0,0), so **Y1 = bit 2**.
- In X4-Y2-Z2, button 2 appears exactly when bit 1 is the same in both stimuli, so **Y2 = bit 1**.
- In X6-Y4-Z3, X3-Y4-Z4 and X5-Y4-Z1, bit 4 separates the buttons, so **Y4 = bit 4**.
- That leaves **Y3 = bit 3**, which fits X1-Y3-Z2.

**X and Z components.** Fixing the bits narrows each rule to a pair of options:
- X5 and X6 are "both are 1" and "not both are 1", in some order.
- Z2 has two possible versions, and each one fixes three rules:
  - **(A)** Z2 gives 3 when true and 2 when false. Then X3 = neither, X4 = exactly one, X1 = same, and X2 = at least one.
  - **(B)** Z2 gives 2 when true and 3 when false. Then X3 = at least one, X4 = same, X1 = exactly one, and X2 = neither.
- Z1 also has two possible versions:
  - **(P)** X5 = both, and Z1 gives 0 when true and 2 when false.
  - **(Q)** X5 = not both, and Z1 gives 2 when true and 0 when false.

All four combinations (A or B with P or Q) fit every example.

**New task X3-Y3-Z1.** This task reads bit 3. Call the case where bit 3 is 0 in both stimuli "neither". The four combinations predict:

| Combination | "Neither" inputs | All other inputs |
|---|---|---|
| A+P | 0 | 2 |
| B+Q | 0 | 2 |
| A+Q | 2 | 0 |
| B+P | 2 | 0 |

So the examples do not determine the answer. Two fitting assignments give one answer set and two give the exact opposite.

**Cross-component patterns.** I looked for a consistent link between "true" and a particular button across the Z components, or a natural ordering of the X versions. Neither assignment family produced a convincing pattern. I chose "neither → 0" (B+Q), but this is close to a coin flip.

The "neither" inputs (bit 3 is 0 in both stimuli) are 4, 8, 10 and 15. They get button 0; all other inputs get button 2.

# Learn tasks from examples

Each task maps an input to one of four buttons: 0, 1, 2, or 3. An input is a pair of stimuli; each stimulus has 4 binary features, written as 4 bits (bit positions 1-4, left to right). The line `1011 0110 -> 2` means: stimulus 1 is 1011, stimulus 2 is 0110, and the correct button is 2.

Every task is built from three components. A **Y component** picks one of the 4 features (bit positions 1-4); the task looks at that feature in both stimuli. An **X component** is a rule on those two bits, one of: both are 1; at least one is 1; exactly one is 1; neither is 1; not both are 1; both are the same. A **Z component** gives one button when the rule is true and a different button when it is false. A task's label lists its components, for example X2-Y1-Z3. Each kind has several versions (X1, X2, and so on); different versions of a kind are different from each other, and the same label always means the same component. You are not told which version does what.
